11  I.   SUMMARY                                                          
12       Plaintiffs1 and Intervenor-Plaintiffs2 in this consolidated case challenge the Bureau 
13  of Land Management of the U.S. Department of Interior3 (“BLM”)’s approval of Intervenor-
14  Defendant Lithium Nevada Corporation’s (“Lithium Nevada”) plan to build a lithium mine 
15  near Thacker Pass, Nevada (the “Project”) under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 
16  U.S.C. § 701, et seq. (“APA”), the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”), 42 U.S.C. 
17  §§ 4321-61, the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (“FLPMA”), 43 U.S.C. §§ 1701-
18  1787, and the National Historic Preservation Act, 54 U.S.C. §§ 300101 (“NHPA”). (ECF 
19  Nos.  1,  46,  83.)  See  also  Western  Watersheds  Project,  et  al.  v.  Bureau  of  Land 
20  Management of the U.S. Department of the Interior, et al., Case No. 3:21-cv-00103-MMD-
21  CLB, ECF No. 1 (D. Nev. Filed Feb. 26, 2021) (since consolidated into this case). Before

25  Basin and Range Watch (collectively, the “Environmental Plaintiffs”).

3  injunction,5 along with an accompanying motion for leave to file a small portion of the 
4  Motion and an exhibit under seal (ECF No. 98).6 Because RSIC and the People have not 
5  met the reconsideration standard, the Court maintains that the Prior Order was correctly 
6  decided, and as further explained below, the Court will deny the Motion.   
7  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
8       A motion to reconsider must set forth “some valid reason why the court should 
9  reconsider its prior decision” and set “forth facts or law of a strongly convincing nature to 
10  persuade the court to reverse its prior decision.” Frasure v. United States, 256 F. Supp. 
11  2d 1180, 1183 (D. Nev. 2003) (citation omitted). Reconsideration is appropriate if this 
12  Court “(1) is presented with newly discovered evidence, (2) committed clear error or the

15  and RSIC and the People filed a reply (ECF No. 107). The Burns Paiute Tribe also joined 
   the Motion. (ECF No. 99.) “The joinder is solely limited to the presentation of new evidence 
16  presented in the Motion regarding the Thacker Pass Massacre Site.” (Id. at 2.)

20  of certain excavations planned as part of the Historic Properties Treatment Plan (“HPTP”). 
   (ECF No. 98 at 1-4.) These redactions appear on pages 24 and 25 of the Motion. (Id. at 
21  3-4.) The motion to seal also seeks to file one exhibit, a map of the Project area with HPTP 
   sites plotted on it, under seal. (Id. at 1-4.) RSIC explains that they have filed this nonpublic

   information  under  seal  because  RSIC  received  it  from  BLM  under  a  confidentiality 
23  agreement, and to protect the location of these culturally sensitive sites from looters, which 
   is why RSIC and BLM entered into the confidentiality agreement in the first place. (Id. at 
24  3.) The Court finds that RSIC has shown compelling reasons to include these limited 
   redactions in its Motion and file one exhibit under seal. See Ctr. for Auto Safety v. Chrysler 
25                                                                        
   Grp., LLC, 809 F.3d 1092, 1101-03 (9th Cir. 2016) (holding that the compelling reasons 
26  standard  applies  to  documents  filed  as  part  of  preliminary  injunction  proceedings). 
   Specifically, the threat of third parties looting sites containing cultural resources is a 
27  compelling reason to keep this material under seal. See, e.g., La Posta Band of Diegueno 
   Mission Indians of La Posta Rsrv. v. Trump, Case No. 320CV01552AJBMSB, 2021 WL 
1  initial decision was manifestly unjust, or (3) if there is an intervening change in controlling 
2  law.” Sch. Dist. No. 1J v. ACandS, Inc., 5 F.3d 1255, 1263 (9th Cir. 1993) (citation omitted). 
3  But “[a] motion for reconsideration is not an avenue to re-litigate the same issues and 
4  arguments upon which the court already has ruled.” Brown v. Kinross Gold, U.S.A., 378 
5  F. Supp. 2d 1280, 1288 (D. Nev. 2005) (citation omitted).             
6       Motions to reconsider are generally left to the discretion of the district court. See 
7  Herbst v. Cook, 260 F.3d 1039, 1044 (9th Cir. 2001). A district court has discretion not to 
8  consider arguments that were not raised until a motion for reconsideration without a good 
9  excuse for the delay. See Rosenfeld v. U.S. Dep’t of Justice, 57 F.3d 803, 811 (9th Cir. 
10  1995); N.W. Acceptance Corp. v. Lynnwood Equip., Inc., 841 F.2d 918, 925-26 (9th Cir. 
11  1988). Moreover, motions for reconsideration are generally not justified on the basis of 
12  new evidence that could have been discovered prior to a district court’s ruling. See Coastal 
13  Transfer Co. v. Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., 833 F.2d 208, 211-12 (9th Cir. 1987). 
14       The  Court  also  incorporates  by  reference  its  recitation  of  the  legal  standard 
15  governing preliminary injunctions from the Prior Order. (ECF No. 92 at 4-5.) 
16  III.  DISCUSSION                                                      
17       RSIC and the People raise two main arguments in their Motion, the first with two 
18  subparts. RSIC and the People first argue the Court clearly erred in: (1) finding the Tribes 
19  lack prudential standing to assert claims on behalf of the Fort McDermitt and Summit Lake 
20  Tribes, and the Winnemucca Indian Colony, who were consulted by BLM and are not 
21  parties to this case; and (2) finding the People lack prudential standing because they are 
22  a subset of the Fort McDermitt Tribe. (ECF No. 96 at 7-19.) Second, the Tribes argue they 
23  have uncovered additional evidence that a massacre occurred near the Project area in the 
24  1860s since they filed their initial motion for a preliminary injunction.7 (Id. at 19-25.) The 
25  Court addresses, and rejects, these two primary arguments below.      
26  ///                                                                   
27

1       A. Prudential Standing                                           
2       RSIC and the People’s arguments that the Court erred in finding that the People 
3  are not a proper party, and the Tribes may not assert inadequate consultation claims under 
4  the NHPA on behalf of the tribes that the BLM did consult, who are not parties to this case, 
5  are unpersuasive on several, alternative levels. First, while it is clear that the Tribes 
6  disagree with the Court’s rulings on these two issues, “[a] motion for reconsideration is not 
7  an avenue to re-litigate the same issues and arguments upon which the court already has 
8  ruled.” Brown, 378 F. Supp. 2d at 1288; see also LR 59-1(b) (noting that motions for 
9  reconsideration are disfavored and parties who repeat arguments may be sanctioned). 
10  The  Tribes  generally  raised  the  same  arguments  they  raise  in  their  Motion  in  the 
11  proceedings on their initial motion for a preliminary injunction, and the Court rejected them 
12  in the Prior Order. (ECF No. 92 at 6-7.) The Court does not find that it erred in these rulings 
13  in  the  Prior  Order,  much  less  that  it  clearly  erred  as  would  be  required  to  make 
14  reconsideration proper.                                               
15       Second, to the extent RSIC and the People are expanding upon their standing 
16  arguments to make arguments they did not assert in connection with the preliminary 
17  injunction proceedings, that too is improper without any explanation—and they offer 
18  none—as to why they did not raise those arguments in the initial proceedings on their 
19  motion for a preliminary injunction. See Rosenfeld, 57 F.3d at 811 (finding that the “district 
20  court did not abuse its discretion in declining to consider an argument raised for the first 
21  time on reconsideration without a good excuse.”).                     
22       Third, RSIC and the People’s challenge to the Court’s finding in the Prior Order that 
23  the People are not a proper party to this case suffers from the additional procedural defect 
24  that the Tribes did not respond to Defendants and Lithium Nevada’s argument on this point 
25  that Defendants and Lithium Nevada raised in in their responses to the Tribes’ preliminary 
26  injunction motion—as the Court noted in the Prior Order. (ECF No. 92 at 6.) Thus, the 
27  Tribes arguably conceded that argument and it would be improper to allow RSIC and the 
1  first time in the Motion. Moreover, the Motion does not address the caselaw the Court 
2  relied on in the Prior Order in finding the People not a proper party to this case. (Compare 
3  id. at 6-7 with ECF No. 96.) To persuasively argue the Court clearly erred, RSIC and the 
4  People should have addressed the law the Court relied on in making one of the findings 
5  they challenge. But they did not.                                     
6       Fourth, RSIC and the People spend much of their Motion and corresponding reply 
7  arguing that they have Article III standing to vindicate the procedural rights of the non-
8  party tribes that BLM did consult with, but the Court never found in the Prior Order that 
9  they lacked Article III standing.8 Indeed, and as should be clear, the Court will address the 
10  merits of RSIC’s claim in its Complaint (ECF No. 46) later this Winter or in early Spring.9 
11  The Court instead found, as a prudential matter, that the Tribes are not proper parties to 
12  assert violations of the rights of the nonparty tribes that BLM did consult. (ECF No. 92 at 
13  6-7.)                                                                 
14       Fifth,  and  relatedly,  there  are  at  least three  different principles that make  up 
15  prudential standing: “the general prohibition on a litigant’s raising another person’s legal 
16  rights,  the  rule  barring  adjudication  of  generalized  grievances  more  appropriately 
17  addressed in the representative branches, and the requirement that a plaintiff’s complaint 
18  fall within the zone of interests protected by the law invoked.” Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static 
19  Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118, 126 (2014). While much of the Motion focuses 
20  on the ‘zone of interests’ principle, the Motion also acknowledges that the Court based its 
21  finding that the Tribes cannot assert violations of the rights of nonparty tribes who were 
22  consulted on the general prohibition on a litigant’s raising another person’s legal rights. 
23  (ECF No. 96 at 14.) Thus, the Court does not further address RSIC and the People’s ‘zone 
24

   inapposite, rendering statements like, “this Court overlooked or misunderstood controlling 
26  Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit precedent” unpersuasive. (ECF No. 96 at 2.)  

27       9Thus, to the extent RSIC and the People argue the Court ‘foreclosed RSIC’s suit,’ 
   RSIC is mistaken. (ECF No. 96 at 12-13.)                              
1  of interests’ arguments that pervade the Motion and instead focuses on RSIC and the 
2  People’s argument as to why the Court erred in its application of the general prohibition 
3  on a litigant raising another person’s legal rights.10 (Id. at 14-16.) This is especially the 
4  case because the Court did not dismiss RSIC’s claims in the Prior Order—it merely denied 
5  the Tribes’ request for a preliminary injunction. (ECF No. 92.) RSIC’s proffered caselaw 
6  regarding the ‘zone of interests’ is also largely inapposite because those cases deal with 
7  appeals of orders dismissing claims entirely. See, e.g., Nulankeyutmonen Nkihtaqmikon 
8  v. Impson, 503 F.3d 18, 25 (1st Cir. 2007) (noting that the district court dismissed for lack 
9  of standing).                                                         
10       Neither Nulankeyutmonen Nkihtaqmikon, 503 F.3d 18, nor the other cases RSIC 
11  relies on in the pertinent portion of its Motion adequately support RSIC’s argument that it 
12  may assert claims on behalf of the nonparty tribes BLM did consult. (ECF No. 96 at 14-
13  16.) RSIC relies on United States v. 0.95 Acres of Land, 994 F.2d 696, 698 (9th Cir. 1993) 
14  for the uncontroversial but irrelevant proposition that “NHPA is similar to NEPA except that 
15  it requires consideration of historic sites, rather than the environment.” Id. (See also ECF 
16  No.  96  at  14-15.)  Tyler  v.  Cuomo,  236  F.3d  1124  (9th  Cir.  2000)  is  similar  to 
17  Nulankeyutmonen Nkihtaqmikon, 503 F.3d 18, in that it is an appeal from a dismissal for 
18  lack of Article III standing. (ECF No. 96 at 15.) And in Lexmark, 572 U.S. at 123, too, the 
19  district court had entirely dismissed the defendant’s counterclaim for a violation of the 
20  Lanham Act. As noted, the Court has never ruled that RSIC lacks Article III standing and 
21  will consider the merits of its claim. But the Court will not consider RSIC’s arguments about 
22  the quality of consultation provided to the nonparty tribes BLM did consult. See, e.g., Coal. 
23                                                                        

24       10The pertinent portion of Montana Wilderness Ass’n v. Fry, 310 F. Supp. 2d 1127, 
   1150-51 (D. Mont. 2004), upon which RSIC again relies (ECF No. 96 at 14) similarly 
25  involved a ‘zone of interests’ analysis regarding Article III standing, which the Court did 
   not engage in in the Prior Order. Moreover, as Defendants note (ECF No. 105 at 8 n.15), 
26  the Court already addressed Fry because the Tribes relied on it in their preliminary 
   injunction motion (see, e.g., ECF No. 45 at 5), and the Court noted in the Prior Order that 
27  it was only explicitly addressing caselaw it found affected the outcome of the order (ECF 
   No. 92 at 22). Moreover, Fry is not binding on this Court in any event, and the Court does 
1  of Clergy, Laws., & Professors v. Bush, 310 F.3d 1153, 1163 (9th Cir. 2002) (“It is a well-
2  established rule that a litigant may assert only his own legal rights and interests and cannot 
3  rest a claim to relief on the legal rights or interests of third parties.”) (citation omitted). 
4       Part of the Court’s concern animating its finding that the Tribes lack prudential 
5  standing to vindicate the rights of the nonparty tribes who were consulted is practical: if 
6  BLM proffers evidence to support its view that its Section 106 consultation with the tribes 
7  it did consult with was adequate, the Tribes allege that it was not but offer no supporting 
8  evidence, and the tribes that BLM actually consulted with are silent, how can the Court 
9  find other than it did in the Prior Order—that the evidence before the Court suggested BLM 
10  complied with its Section 106 and public consultation obligations? (ECF No. 92 at 17.) It 
11  would  be  improper  for  the  Court  to  make  an  evidentiary  finding  without  necessary 
12  evidence. That evidence would have to come from the third-party tribes. Said otherwise, 
13  the Court would prefer to hear from the tribes that BLM actually consulted to find out 
14  whether they thought BLM’s Section 106 consultation with them regarding the Project was 
15  sufficient instead of the Tribes, who were undisputedly not consulted.11 
16       Another aspect of the Court’s prudential standing findings—particularly as to the 
17  People—relates to the implementing regulations of the NHPA upon which the Tribes rely. 
18  36  C.F.R.  §  800.2(c)(2)(ii)(C)  states  that  BLM  “must  recognize  the  government-to-
19  government  relationship  between  the  Federal  Government  and  Indian  tribes”  and 
20  therefore “consult with representatives designated or identified by the tribal government.” 
21  That representative cannot be the People because the People are all members of the Fort 
22  McDermitt Paiute and Shoshone Tribe. (ECF No. 92 at 6-7.) And here, BLM sent a 
23  consultation letter to Chairman Tildon Smart of the Fort McDermitt Tribe. (ECF No. 65-8 
24  at 2-4.) If Chairman Smart designated the People as representatives of the Fort McDermitt 
25                                                                        

26       11The Court found the Tribes were unlikely to prevail on the merits of their claim 
   that BLM’s decision not to consult them was unreasonable in the Prior Order, and RSIC 
27  and the People’s Motion does not challenge that finding. (ECF No. 92 at 7-18; see also 
   generally ECF No. 96.)                                                
1  Tribe, the People presumably would have offered some argument or evidence to this 
2  effect. They did not. Further, the People presumably disagree with Chairman Smart’s 
3  decision not to respond to that letter because they moved to intervene in this case. 
4  However, it seems improper under these implementing regulations for the Court to wade 
5  into a dispute about whether to support or oppose the Project amongst members of the 
6  Fort McDermitt Tribe12 because that could be perceived as disregarding the government-
7  to-government relationship between the federal government and the Fort McDermitt Tribe. 
8  See 36 C.F.R. § 800.2(c)(2)(ii)(C). The Court does not wish to do that.  
9       In sum, and for the reasons provided above, the Court declines to reconsider its 
10  decisions that the People are not a proper party to this case, and RSIC may not argue that 
11  BLM violated the consultation rights of the tribes it did consult with. 
12       B. Additional Evidence                                           
13       RSIC and the Burns Paiute Tribe13 also proffer additional evidence supporting their 
14  view that it is likely some victims of an 1865 massacre of Paiutes perpetrated by the 1st 
15  Nevada Cavalry that occurred near the Project area likely fled into the Project area, so 
16  their remains may be somewhere within the Project area.14 (ECF No. 96 at 21-25.) While 
17  the Court agrees with RSIC and the Burns Paiute Tribe that this additional evidence further 
18  highlights the shameful history of the treatment of Native Americans by federal and state 
19  governments, it does not persuade the Court that it should reconsider the irreparable harm 
20  findings of the Prior Order. (ECF No. 92 at 18-22.)

   and Lithium Nevada proffered a declaration from one member of the Fort McDermitt Tribe 
24  who disagrees with the People and thinks the Project should move ahead. (ECF No. 66-
   10.)

        13As noted, they joined this portion of the Motion. (ECF No. 99.)   
26                                                                        
        14RSIC also argues the Court overlooked its irreparable procedural harm argument. 
27  (ECF No. 96 at 19-21.) The Court disagrees. The Court mentioned that the Tribes made 
   this argument (ECF No. 92 at 18-19) but did not find it materially affected the outcome the 
1       First,  and  as  Defendants  and  Lithium  Nevada  argue,  the  Tribes  could  have 
2  presented this new evidence with their preliminary injunction motion, as it is over 100 years 
3  old, but did not. While of course a preliminary injunction proceeding is different from, say, 
4  summary  judgment  proceedings  in  that  the  factual  record  is  necessarily  less  well-
5  developed, the fact that the Tribes did not present this evidence with their initial motion 
6  nonetheless  weighs  against  considering  it  on  reconsideration.  See,  e.g.,  Marlyn 
7  Nutraceuticals, Inc. v. Mucos Pharma GmbH & Co., 571 F.3d 873, 880-81 (9th Cir. 2009) 
8  (finding the district court did not abuse its discretion in denying a motion for reconsideration 
9  of an order granting a preliminary injunction on the basis of new evidence where the party 
10  could have  introduced  that evidence  before  the  district  court entered  its preliminary 
11  injunction order but did not). Generally speaking, a party must make a showing of diligence 
12  to support a request for reconsideration based on newly discovered evidence that could 
13  have been discovered earlier. See ACandS, Inc., 5 F.3d at 1263 (“The overwhelming 
14  weight of authority is that the failure to file documents in an original motion or opposition 
15  does not turn the late filed documents into ‘newly discovered evidence.”’) (citation omitted); 
16  Wallis v. J.R. Simplot Co., 26 F.3d 885, 892 n.6 (9th Cir. 1994), as amended on denial of 
17  reh’g (July 14, 1994) (“Evidence is not newly discovered if it was in the party’s possession 
18  at  the  time  of  summary  judgment  or  could  have  been  discovered  with  reasonable 
19  diligence.”). The fact that the Motion does not even refer to RSIC’s diligence in locating 
20  the purported newly discovered evidence tends to weigh against reconsideration. 
21       Second, RSIC’s proffered newly discovered evidence is cumulative of the evidence 
22  the Court already considered and found did not sufficiently support issuing a preliminary 
23  injunction. The Tribes proffered evidence that a massacre occurred near the Project area 
24  in the 1860s in the preliminary injunction proceedings, but the Court found that evidence 
25  did not show a massacre occurred within the Project area, especially considering that 
26  there has been significant ground disturbance within the Project area for some time that 
27  had never located any human remains and there are plans in place to address the 
1  below, RSIC’s proffered newly discovered evidence does not definitely establish that a 
2  massacre occurred within the Project area. Thus, it does not persuade the Court to 
3  reconsider the Prior Order. See La Posta Band of Diegueno Mission Indians, 2021 WL 
4  51454, at *2-*4 (denying motion for reconsideration based on purported new evidence of 
5  the government’s decision to treat arguably animal bone fragments as if they were human 
6  and an additional, inadvertent discovery of a fire ring in part because the purported new 
7  evidence  was  cumulative  of  the  evidence  the  district  court  considered  in  the  initial 
8  preliminary injunction proceedings).                                  
9       Third, and even on RSIC’s own terms, the proffered newly discovered evidence is 
10  too speculative to support an irreparable harm finding. RSIC begins its argument by 
11  arguing that the newly discovered evidence makes it “much more likely” that a massacre 
12  occurred in the Project area. (ECF No. 96 at 21.) RSIC goes on to confirm the evidence 
13  considered and discussed in the Prior Order showed that the camps of the Paiutes who 
14  were massacred were near, but not in, the Project area. (Id. at 21.) RSIC then argues its 
15  newly discovered evidence “make[s] it very likely that the September 12, 1865 massacre 
16  happened, at least partially, within the project area.” (Id.) RSIC later describes how a newly 
17  proffered map shows “how close excavation will occur to the Paiute camps,” meaning that, 
18  “[t]hese excavation sites are also likely within the massacre site.” (Id. at 24.) Contrary to 
19  RSIC’s argument (id. at 25), this is insufficiently specific evidence of irreparable harm. The 
20  pertinent  portion  of  the  Motion  is  couched  in  possibility—RSIC  deliberately  avoids 
21  statements of certainty. Accordingly, even if the Court were to consider RSIC’s newly 
22  discovered evidence, it is too speculative to support an irreparable harm finding sufficient 
23  to grant a preliminary injunction. See Caribbean Marine Servs. Co. v. Baldrige, 844 F.2d 
24  668, 674 (9th Cir. 1988) (“Speculative injury does not constitute irreparable injury sufficient 
25  to warrant granting a preliminary injunction.”) (citation omitted).   
26       The Court therefore declines to reconsider the Prior Order and will deny the Motion.
